claim: The concept of objects is fundamental to cognition and is defined by a consistent set of sensory properties and physical affordances.
source: The concept of objects is fundamental to cognition and is defined by a consistent set of sensory properties and physical affordances.
evidence: This is a general statement about cognitive science that draws from established understanding in the field.

claim: It is unknown how the abstract concept of an object emerges.
source: Although it is unknown how the abstract concept of an object emerges, most accounts assume that visual or haptic boundaries are crucial in this process.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Most accounts assume that visual or haptic boundaries are crucial in the process of object concept emergence.
source: Although it is unknown how the abstract concept of an object emerges, most accounts assume that visual or haptic boundaries are crucial in this process.
evidence: This refers to existing theoretical accounts in the field.

claim: Participants showed strong within-modality learning in the visuo-haptic statistical learning paradigm.
source: Participants showed strong within-modality learning and 'zero-shot' across-modality generalisation which were highly correlated.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Participants showed 'zero-shot' across-modality generalisation in the visuo-haptic statistical learning paradigm.
source: Participants showed strong within-modality learning and 'zero-shot' across-modality generalisation which were highly correlated.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Within-modality learning and across-modality generalisation were highly correlated.
source: Participants showed strong within-modality learning and 'zero-shot' across-modality generalisation which were highly correlated.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Humans can segment scenes into objects without any explicit boundary cues using purely statistical information.
source: Our results demonstrate that humans can segment scenes into objects, without any explicit boundary cues, using purely statistical information.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The coherent organization of information across different modalities is crucial for efficiently interacting with the world.
source: The coherent organization of information across different modalities is crucial for efficiently interacting with the world and lies at the heart of the concept of what defines an object (Amedi et al., 2001; Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001; Streri and Spelke, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The coherent organization of information across different modalities lies at the heart of the concept of what defines an object.
source: The coherent organization of information across different modalities is crucial for efficiently interacting with the world and lies at the heart of the concept of what defines an object (Amedi et al., 2001; Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001; Streri and Spelke, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Classic theories place visual boundaries, edges and contrast transitions at the very core of the process by which we segment objects from the environment.
source: Classic theories place visual boundaries, edges and contrast transitions, at the very core of the process by which we segment objects from the environment (Marr, 1982; Peterson, 1994; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Spelke, 1990; von der Heydt et al., 1984; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to classic theories.

claim: Boundary cues are insufficient for successful segmentation alone as they can both lead to false object boundaries within objects and miss boundaries between objects.
source: However, such boundary cues are insufficient for successful segmentation alone as they can both lead to false object boundaries within objects (e.g. the stripes of a zebra) and miss boundaries between objects (e.g. the illusory contours of the Kanizsa triangle).
evidence: This is supported by examples from visual perception (zebra stripes, Kanizsa triangle) which are well-known phenomena.

claim: Statistical learning mechanisms are sensitive to the co-occurrence statistics of individual constituent elements.
source: Statistical learning mechanisms, sensitive to the co-occurrence statistics of individual constituent elements (syllables, shapes, etc), have been demonstrated to be capable of segmenting inputs even when low-level segmentation cues were entirely uninformative (Aslin et al., 1998; Fiser and Aslin, 2005; Orbán et al., 2008; Saffran et al., 1996)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Statistical learning mechanisms have been demonstrated to be capable of segmenting inputs even when low-level segmentation cues were entirely uninformative.
source: Statistical learning mechanisms, sensitive to the co-occurrence statistics of individual constituent elements (syllables, shapes, etc), have been demonstrated to be capable of segmenting inputs even when low-level segmentation cues were entirely uninformative (Aslin et al., 1998; Fiser and Aslin, 2005; Orbán et al., 2008; Saffran et al., 1996)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is unknown whether the representations created by statistical learning go beyond forming abstract 'units' or lead to real object-like representations.
source: but it is unknown whether the representations they create go beyond forming abstract 'units' (formalised as latent causes; Gershman and Niv, 2010; Orbán et al., 2008) or lead to real object-like representations.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Under natural conditions, boundary cues and edges can be correlated with the statistical contingencies of objects.
source: This avoided the problem that, under natural conditions, boundary cues and edges can be correlated with the statistical contingencies of objects (Geisler et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A minimal requirement for what an object is is 'a material thing that can be seen and touched'.
source: As a minimal requirement for what an object is — 'a material thing that can be seen and touched' (Oxford Dictionaries, 2017)
evidence: This is a definition cited from Oxford Dictionaries.

claim: Participants should be able to predict haptic properties of objects based on just visual statistics without any prior haptic experience with them and without receiving any form of feedback in the generalisation task.
source: That is, participants should be able to predict haptic properties of objects based on just visual statistics, without any prior haptic experience with them and without receiving any form of feedback in the generalisation task, and vica versa, they should be able to predict visual properties based on haptic statistical exposure alone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that the study tests.

claim: Participants should be able to predict visual properties based on haptic statistical exposure alone.
source: That is, participants should be able to predict haptic properties of objects based on just visual statistics, without any prior haptic experience with them and without receiving any form of feedback in the generalisation task, and vica versa, they should be able to predict visual properties based on haptic statistical exposure alone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that the study tests.

claim: Each object in the inventory was defined as a unique pair of unfamiliar shapes.
source: We created an inventory of artificial 'objects', such that each object was defined as a unique pair of unfamiliar shapes (Figure 1A, inventory, colouring and gaps within pseudo pairs for illustration only).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Only the individual shapes, but not the pairs defining the objects of the inventory, had visible boundaries.
source: Note that only the individual shapes, but not the pairs defining the objects of the inventory, had visible boundaries.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Boundary cues were uninformative with regard to the object identities in the experimental paradigm.
source: Therefore, boundary cues were uninformative with regard to the object identities, and instead participants could only rely on the statistical contingencies among the shapes that we created in either the visual or the haptic modality during an exposure phase.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Participants could only rely on the statistical contingencies among the shapes created in either the visual or the haptic modality during an exposure phase.
source: Therefore, boundary cues were uninformative with regard to the object identities, and instead participants could only rely on the statistical contingencies among the shapes that we created in either the visual or the haptic modality during an exposure phase.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed significantly above chance in the visual familiarity test after visual exposure.
source: In line with previous results (Fiser and Aslin, 2005; Fiser and Aslin, 2001), we found that mere visual observation of the exposure scenes enabled participants to perform significantly above chance in the visual familiarity test (Figure 2A, black dots: visual familiarity performance for individuals quantified by fraction correct, green dot and error bar: group average 0.77 [95% CI: 0.67–0.87], t(19) = 5.66, p=1.9⋅10−5, Bayes factor = 1253).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mere visual observation of the exposure scenes enabled participants to perform significantly above chance in the visual familiarity test.
source: In line with previous results (Fiser and Aslin, 2005; Fiser and Aslin, 2001), we found that mere visual observation of the exposure scenes enabled participants to perform significantly above chance in the visual familiarity test (Figure 2A, black dots: visual familiarity performance for individuals quantified by fraction correct, green dot and error bar: group average 0.77 [95% CI: 0.67–0.87], t(19) = 5.66, p=1.9⋅10−5, Bayes factor = 1253).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In novel test scenes participants judged 'true pairs' more familiar than 'pseudo pairs', despite having seen all constituent shapes an equal number of times.
source: That is, in novel test scenes participants judged 'true pairs' more familiar than 'pseudo pairs', despite having seen all constituent shapes an equal number of times.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Exposure to visual statistical contingencies generalised to participants' judgements as to the force required to pull apart novel compound objects.
source: Critically, the exposure to visual statistical contingencies also generalised to participants' judgements as to the force required to pull apart novel compound objects.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants performed significantly above chance in the haptic pulling test after visual exposure.
source: Participants performed significantly above chance (Figure 2A, black dots: haptic pulling performance for individuals, blue dot and error bar: group average ρ = 0.27 [95% CI: 0.07–0.47], t(19) = 2.88, p=0.0095, Bayes factor = 5; see also Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 3A.

claim: Going from random haptic pulling performance (ρ = 0) to perfect performance (ρ = 1) covered 87% of the possible range of visual familiarity performance (fraction correct from 0.5 to 1.0).
source: In particular, our fit of the data revealed that going from random haptic pulling performance (ρ = 0) to perfect performance (ρ = 1) covered 87% of the possible range of visual familiarity performance (fraction correct from 0.5 to 1.0).
evidence: This is derived from the statistical model fit to the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant trend in performance throughout the haptic pulling test trials after visual exposure.
source: We also tested whether there was a significant change in performance throughout the haptic pulling test trials and found no significant trend (p=0.07, Bayes factor = 1, see Materials and methods) suggesting that generalisation immediately appeared and it did not just gradually develop during the test.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Generalisation immediately appeared and did not just gradually develop during the test after visual exposure.
source: We also tested whether there was a significant change in performance throughout the haptic pulling test trials and found no significant trend (p=0.07, Bayes factor = 1, see Materials and methods) suggesting that generalisation immediately appeared and it did not just gradually develop during the test.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis showing no significant trend.

claim: Participants successfully generalised what they learned through visual statistics to predict the haptic properties of objects.
source: These results show that participants successfully generalised what they learned through visual statistics to predict the haptic properties of objects, and suggest that variability in performance on both tasks across participants is due to the same underlying cause: differences in how well participants learned the inventory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Variability in performance on both tasks across participants is due to the same underlying cause: differences in how well participants learned the inventory.
source: These results show that participants successfully generalised what they learned through visual statistics to predict the haptic properties of objects, and suggest that variability in performance on both tasks across participants is due to the same underlying cause: differences in how well participants learned the inventory.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between performance on the two tasks.

claim: Infants have been shown to learn to segment visual scenes or auditory streams automatically after mere passive exposure.
source: Although our experiments were conducted with adult participants, infants have also been shown to learn to segment visual scenes or auditory streams automatically, after mere passive exposure (Fiser and Aslin, 2002; Kirkham et al., 2002; Quinn and Bhatt, 2005; Saffran and Kirkham, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on infant learning.

claim: Infant studies used stimuli with a statistical structure similar or identical to those used in the current experiment.
source: Importantly, these studies used stimuli with a statistical structure (and in the case of visual experiments, actual constituent shapes) that were similar or even identical to those used in our experiment (Fiser and Aslin, 2002; Quinn and Bhatt, 2005; Saffran et al., 1996; Saffran and Kirkham, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on infant learning.

claim: By parsimony, infants possess the same sensitivity to the co-occurrence statistics of sensory inputs as adults.
source: This suggests that, by parsimony, infants possess the same sensitivity to the co-occurrence statistics of sensory inputs as adults (Aslin, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of stimuli used in infant and adult studies, supported by a citation.

claim: Statistical learning mechanisms revealed in the current experiments might also operate in the emergence of object representations during cognitive development.
source: Since we showed that statistical learning produces object-like representations in adults, we propose that the statistical learning mechanisms revealed in our experiments might also operate in the emergence of object representations during cognitive development.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and previous infant research.

claim: Participants performed significantly above chance in the haptic pulling test after haptic exposure.
source: Performance on the haptic pulling test showed that participants successfully learned which scenes required more or less pulling force (Figure 2B, black dots: haptic pulling performance for individuals, blue dot and error bar: group average ρ = 0.28 [95% CI: 0.14–0.42], t(19) = 4.34, p=3.8⋅10−3, Bayes factor = 91; see also Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3B.

claim: Haptic experience affected participants' judgements in the visual familiarity test.
source: Haptic experience also affected participants' judgements in the visual familiarity test, in which they needed to compare two pairs, one a true pair and the other a pseudo pair.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants judged true pairs significantly more familiar than pseudo pairs after haptic exposure.
source: Participants judged true pairs significantly more familiar than pseudo pairs (Figure 2B, black dots: visual familiarity performance for individuals, green dot and error bar: group average quantified by fraction correct 0.6 [95% CI: 0.51–0.69], t(19) = 2.2, p=0.038).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the haptic exposure experiment, haptic and visual statistics were in explicit conflict.
source: Note that this across-modality effect was even weaker on average than previously (Bayes factor = 2 indicates evidence that is weak or not worth mentioning) because, in contrast to the previous experiment, haptic and visual statistics were now in explicit conflict: true and pseudo pairs (compared in the visual familiarity task) were identical in their visual statistics and only differed in their haptic statistics.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: True and pseudo pairs were identical in their visual statistics and only differed in their haptic statistics in the haptic exposure experiment.
source: Note that this across-modality effect was even weaker on average than previously (Bayes factor = 2 indicates evidence that is weak or not worth mentioning) because, in contrast to the previous experiment, haptic and visual statistics were now in explicit conflict: true and pseudo pairs (compared in the visual familiarity task) were identical in their visual statistics and only differed in their haptic statistics.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: There was no significant change in performance throughout the familiarity test trials after haptic exposure.
source: As before, there was no significant change in performance throughout the familiarity test trials (p=0.58, Bayes factor <1, see Materials and methods) suggesting that the generalisation effect did not gradually emerge during the test trials.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The generalisation effect did not gradually emerge during the test trials after haptic exposure.
source: As before, there was no significant change in performance throughout the familiarity test trials (p=0.58, Bayes factor <1, see Materials and methods) suggesting that the generalisation effect did not gradually emerge during the test trials.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis showing no significant trend.

claim: Objects that appeared precisely the same number of times as others were 'illusorily' but systematically perceived as visually more familiar just because they had more object-like haptic properties.
source: That is, objects that appeared precisely the same number of times as others were 'illusorily' but systematically perceived as visually more familiar just because they had more object-like haptic properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the haptic exposure experiment.

claim: Similar levels of haptic performance were found in the two experiments.
source: Interestingly, we found similar levels of haptic performance in the two experiments (t(18) = 0.09, p=0.93, Bayes factor (favouring the same performance levels)=3, see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of data across the two experiments.

claim: In the first experiment there was no haptic statistical exposure at all and participants' haptic performance relied only on generalisation from the visual exposure.
source: even though in the first experiment there was no haptic statistical exposure at all and participants' haptic performance relied only on generalisation from the visual exposure.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Performance on the visual familiarity test was higher after visual exposure than after haptic exposure.
source: Performance on the visual familiarity test was higher after visual exposure than after haptic exposure (t(18) = 2.65, p=0.01, Bayes factor (favouring different performance levels)=4)
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of data across the two experiments.

claim: The difference in visual familiarity performance between experiments was expected based on the fundamental difference in cue conflicts between the two experiments.
source: which was expected based on the fundamental difference in cue conflicts between the two experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design differences.

claim: A within-participant analysis found significantly positive consistency between familiarity and pulling force for individual scenes.
source: We found a significantly positive consistency (correlation 0.297 ± 0.104 with t(34) = 2.86, p=0.007, Bayes factor = 6).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of within-participant data pooled across both experiments.

claim: Participants developed a modality-generic representation of objects from either visual or haptic statistical contingencies alone, which they could transfer to the other modality.
source: Taken together, this demonstrates that participants developed a modality-generic representation of objects from either visual or haptic statistical contingencies alone, which in turn they could transfer to the other modality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the within-participant consistency analysis.

claim: Across participants, the performance in the visual familiarity and in the haptic pulling test strongly correlated.
source: Across these participants, the performance in the visual familiarity and in the haptic pulling test strongly correlated (R = 0.84 [95% CI: 0.65–0.93], p=6.2⋅10−7, Bayes factor = 3225, see also Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of debriefing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When controlling for participants' explicit knowledge, there was still a highly significant partial correlation between visual and haptic performance.
source: Critically, when we controlled for participants' explicit knowledge (proportion of correctly identified pairs) on the relationship between visual and haptic performance, we still found a highly significant partial correlation (R = 0.69 [95% CI: 0.38–0.86], p=3.1⋅10−4, Bayes factor = 23.4, see also Figure 4C) suggesting strong implicit transfer between modalities in addition to that afforded by this kind of explicit knowledge.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of debriefing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Strong implicit transfer between modalities exists in addition to that afforded by explicit knowledge.
source: Critically, when we controlled for participants' explicit knowledge (proportion of correctly identified pairs) on the relationship between visual and haptic performance, we still found a highly significant partial correlation (R = 0.69 [95% CI: 0.38–0.86], p=3.1⋅10−4, Bayes factor = 23.4, see also Figure 4C) suggesting strong implicit transfer between modalities in addition to that afforded by this kind of explicit knowledge.
evidence: This is an inference from the partial correlation analysis.

claim: The larger part (67%) of the generalisation effect is due to implicit transfer and cannot be explained by explicit reasoning about the pairs.
source: Furthermore, the ratio of the explained variances (R2) shows that the larger part (67%) of the generalisation effect is due to implicit transfer and cannot be explained by explicit reasoning about the pairs.
evidence: This is derived from comparing the explained variances of the normal and partial correlations.

claim: Participants could segment scenes into objects based on either visual or haptic statistics alone, without any boundaries that could identify the objects.
source: In summary, we found evidence that participants could segment scenes into objects based on either visual or haptic statistics alone, without any boundaries that could identify the objects.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: Such learning led to genuinely coherent object-like representations as participants segmented scenes into objects consistently across the two modalities.
source: Such learning led to genuinely coherent object-like representations as participants segmented scenes into objects consistently across the two modalities, independent of the modality in which the statistics of the objects were originally experienced.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: Participants segmented scenes into objects consistently across the two modalities, independent of the modality in which the statistics of the objects were originally experienced.
source: Such learning led to genuinely coherent object-like representations as participants segmented scenes into objects consistently across the two modalities, independent of the modality in which the statistics of the objects were originally experienced.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: Implicit statistical learning over short periods is known to be difficult.
source: Our participants' within- and across-modality performance was not perfect as implicit statistical learning over short periods is known to be difficult (Kim et al., 2009; Perruchet and Pacton, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Participants who learned well within one modality showed strong generalisation to the other modality, beyond what an explicit sense of knowledge of the objects would have predicted.
source: However, critically, participants who learned well within one modality showed strong generalisation to the other modality (Figure 2), beyond what an explicit sense of knowledge of the objects, potentially leading to highly cognitive strategies, would have predicted (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Earlier reports in statistical learning only showed that statistical cues can be used for segmentation in various sensory modalities.
source: Earlier reports in statistical learning only showed that statistical cues can be used for segmentation (in various sensory modalities).
evidence: This characterizes previous research in the field.

claim: Previous statistical learning studies typically focused on a single modality.
source: However, they typically focused on a single modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2005; Creel et al., 2004; Fiser and Aslin, 2001; Hunt and Aslin, 2001)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies showed that humans can combine statistical information simultaneously presented in more than one modality.
source: or showed that humans can combine statistical information simultaneously presented in more than one modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous statistical learning studies did not investigate the 'objectness' of the resulting representations in any way.
source: Critically, these studies did not investigate the 'objectness' of the resulting representations in any way.
evidence: This characterizes a limitation of previous research.

claim: Previous studies did not test generalisation across modalities and hence could not exclude the possibility that performance in each modality only relied on information presented in that modality alone.
source: In particular, they did not test generalisation across modalities and hence could not exclude the possibility that performance in each modality only relied on information presented in that modality alone, without an underlying modality-general object-like representation.
evidence: This characterizes a limitation of previous research.

claim: Other studies showed generalisation across visual and haptic modalities, but they used objects which were already fully segmented by low-level boundary cues.
source: Conversely, other studies showed generalisation across visual and haptic modalities, but they used objects which were already fully segmented by low-level boundary cues and as such they could not investigate the role of statistical learning in the emergence of object-like representations (Yildirim and Jacobs, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous cross-modal studies could not investigate the role of statistical learning in the emergence of object-like representations.
source: Conversely, other studies showed generalisation across visual and haptic modalities, but they used objects which were already fully segmented by low-level boundary cues and as such they could not investigate the role of statistical learning in the emergence of object-like representations (Yildirim and Jacobs, 2013).
evidence: This characterizes a limitation of previous research.

claim: The findings suggest a deeper underlying integration of object-like representations obtained by statistical learning: any statistically defined structural information obtained in one modality becomes automatically integrated into a general internal representation linking multiple modalities.
source: Instead, our findings suggest a deeper underlying integration of object-like representations obtained by statistical learning: any statistically defined structural information obtained in one modality becomes automatically integrated into a general internal representation linking multiple modalities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The statistical learning mechanisms revealed in the experiments might also operate in the emergence of object representations during cognitive development.
source: If, as we argue, the statistical learning mechanisms we revealed also operate in infants, the present findings complement the results of earlier infant studies on object representations.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and previous infant research.

claim: Previous studies of cognitive development defined a specific set of criteria, including cohesion, boundedness, rigidity, and no action at a distance, that infants use to identify objects.
source: In contrast, previous studies of cognitive development defined a specific set of criteria, including cohesion, boundedness, rigidity, and no action at a distance, that infants use to identify objects (Kellman and Spelke, 1983; Spelke, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results suggest that the classical criteria for object identification may be sufficient but not necessary.
source: Our results suggest that these criteria may be sufficient but not necessary.
evidence: This is an inference from the current findings in relation to previous theories.

claim: The objects in the experiment violated the basic requirement of having 3-dimensional structure.
source: For example, one might argue that the objects in our experiment violated even the basic requirement of having 3-dimensional structure, and specifically the principle of 'cohesion' of Spelke (1990) because their constituent shapes were separated by gaps (although in front of a spatially contiguous grey background).
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design in relation to classical object criteria.

claim: The classical criteria for object identification may be special cases of a more general principle of statistical coherence.
source: Thus, these classical criteria may be special cases of a more general principle of statistical coherence.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the current findings.

claim: An internal object-like representation segmented based on statistical coherence may need to eventually pass a number of additional criteria to become a real mental object.
source: Nevertheless, an internal object-like representation segmented based on statistical coherence (and other cues) may need to eventually pass a number of additional criteria (e.g. those involving cohesion) to become a real mental object, and it will be for future studies to test whether and how statistical learning mechanisms can produce such representations.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: There may be many shades of perceiving 'objectness' ranging from rigid bodies through more elusive entities to collections of clearly separate objects.
source: In general, there may be many shades of perceiving 'objectness' (ranging from rigid bodies through more elusive entities, such as a melting scoop of ice cream or the jet of steam of a boiling teapot, to collections of clearly separate objects).
evidence: This is a general observation about the concept of objectness.

claim: Further work will be needed to refine the necessary and sufficient conditions for segmenting entities with different degrees of objectness.
source: Thus, further work will be needed to refine the necessary and sufficient conditions for segmenting entities with different degrees of objectness on this continuum.
evidence: This identifies a direction for future research.

claim: The difference in the behavioural measures used to index object perception in previous studies and in the current experiments may need more attention.
source: Similarly, the difference in the behavioural measures used to index object perception in previous studies and in our experiments (looking times vs. across-modality generalisation) may also need more attention.
evidence: This identifies a methodological consideration for future research.

claim: The current work represents an important first step in connecting the field of statistical learning to the kind of object representations that have been identified in infants.
source: From this perspective, our work represents an important first step in connecting the field of statistical learning to the kind of object representations that have been identified in infants.
evidence: This is a characterization of the contribution of the current work.

claim: The present study does not provide empirical evidence for a single specific cognitive mechanism underlying the generalisation effects found.
source: Finally, although the present study does not provide empirical evidence for a single specific cognitive mechanism underlying the generalisation effects we found, these results together with previous studies (Lake et al., 2015; Orbán et al., 2008) point to possible computations explaining the present findings.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: The results together with previous studies point to possible computations explaining the present findings.
source: Finally, although the present study does not provide empirical evidence for a single specific cognitive mechanism underlying the generalisation effects we found, these results together with previous studies (Lake et al., 2015; Orbán et al., 2008) point to possible computations explaining the present findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous research.

claim: The generalisation effects occurred without any ancillary cues that are required to engage specialized learning mechanisms.
source: First, the generalisation effects occurred without any ancillary cues that are required to engage specialized learning mechanisms, such as segmentation cues for implicit rule learning (Peña et al., 2002; Saffran et al., 2007), verbal instructions for explicit hypothesis testing (Shanks, 2010), or ostensive signals for social learning (Csibra and Gergely, 2006).
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is unlikely that participants were able to retain in memory all the raw sensory stimuli they received during the exposure phase.
source: Second, it is unlikely that participants were able to retain in memory all the raw sensory stimuli they received during the exposure phase (e.g., 444 scenes with six shapes in each for the statistical exposure experiment).
evidence: This is an inference based on the large number of stimuli presented.

claim: Participants must have developed some compressed representation of the stimuli during exposure.
source: Thus, they must have developed some compressed representation of those stimuli during exposure, and it is only this representation that then could allow them to generalise in the test phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that participants could not retain all raw stimuli.

claim: Statistical learning goes beyond the learning of simple (pairwise) associations between the constituent components of objects.
source: Third, with regard to the form of the compressed representation, statistical learning goes beyond the learning of simple (pairwise) associations between the constituent components of objects, and has been shown to be best described as the extraction of statistically meaningful (potentially multivariate) latent 'chunks' (Gershman and Niv, 2010; Orbán et al., 2008; Yildirim and Jacobs, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Statistical learning has been shown to be best described as the extraction of statistically meaningful latent 'chunks'.
source: Third, with regard to the form of the compressed representation, statistical learning goes beyond the learning of simple (pairwise) associations between the constituent components of objects, and has been shown to be best described as the extraction of statistically meaningful (potentially multivariate) latent 'chunks' (Gershman and Niv, 2010; Orbán et al., 2008; Yildirim and Jacobs, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Latent chunks are the abstract representations that are built automatically during exposure and mediate the across-modality effects observed.
source: Therefore, we propose that these latent chunks are the abstract representations that are built automatically during exposure and mediate the across-modality effects we observed.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and previous research on statistical learning.

claim: Accumulating evidence supports the view that the neural representation underlying multimodal integration might involve cortical areas traditionally linked to unimodal processing.
source: Accumulating evidence supports this view by showing that the neural representation underlying multimodal integration might involve cortical areas traditionally linked to unimodal processing (Amedi et al., 2001; Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous neuroscience research.

claim: Statistical learning is a domain-general mechanism.
source: Together, these results suggest that statistical learning is not only a domain-general mechanism (Frost et al., 2015; Kirkham et al., 2002; Thiessen, 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Statistical learning results in domain-general internal representations that could be the basis for the emergence of affordances and the abstraction of object concepts.
source: but it also results in domain-general internal representations that could be the basis for the emergence of affordances (Gibson, 1979; Parker and Gibson, 1977) and the abstraction of object concepts (Carey, 2011; Leslie et al., 1998; Spelke, 1990).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and previous research, supported by citations.

claim: In the visual statistical exposure experiment, 28 participants gave informed consent and participated.
source: In the visual statistical exposure experiment, 28 participants (age range 19–39, mean 25, 20 women) gave informed consent and participated.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Eight participants were excluded from full analysis in the visual statistical exposure experiment as they did not achieve significant performance in haptic task training.
source: Eight participants were excluded from full analysis as they did not achieve significant performance in haptic task training (see below, 'Exclusion criteria').
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied.

claim: The final sample in the visual statistical exposure experiment comprised of 20 participants.
source: The final sample therefore comprised of 20 participants (age range 20–39, mean 25, 15 women).
evidence: This describes the final participant sample after exclusions.

claim: In the haptic statistical exposure experiment, 20 participants gave informed consent and participated.
source: In the haptic statistical exposure experiment, 20 participants (age range 21–34, mean 26, 16 women) gave informed consent and participated.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: No participants were excluded in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: No participants were excluded (see below, 'Exclusion criteria').
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the University of Cambridge Psychology Ethics Committee.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the University of Cambridge Psychology Ethics Committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Two vBOTs were used to provide haptic stimuli and record haptic responses.
source: We used two vBOTs to provide haptic stimuli and record haptic responses (during haptic exposure and testing, respectively).
evidence: This describes the experimental equipment.

claim: The vBOT is a custom-built back-drivable planar robotic manipulandum exhibiting low mass at its handle.
source: The vBOT is a custom-built back-drivable planar robotic manipulandum exhibiting low mass at its handle, with the handle position measured using optical encoders sampled at 1000 Hz, and torque motors allowing endpoint forces to be specified (Howard et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental equipment with a citation.

claim: Visual stimuli consisted of 12 black abstract geometric shapes in the visual statistical exposure experiment.
source: In both experiments, following previous work (Fiser and Aslin, 2001), visual stimuli for statistical learning consisted of 12 (visual statistical exposure experiment) or 8 (haptic statistical exposure experiment) black abstract geometric shapes of intermediate complexity arranged along a regular grid (without grid lines shown) on a grey background (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Visual stimuli consisted of 8 black abstract geometric shapes in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: In both experiments, following previous work (Fiser and Aslin, 2001), visual stimuli for statistical learning consisted of 12 (visual statistical exposure experiment) or 8 (haptic statistical exposure experiment) black abstract geometric shapes of intermediate complexity arranged along a regular grid (without grid lines shown) on a grey background (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The shapes were grouped into 'true pairs' such that constituent shapes of a pair were always shown together and in the same spatial arrangement.
source: Unbeknownst to participants, the shapes were grouped into 'true pairs' (the 'objects'), such that constituent shapes of a pair were always shown together and in the same spatial (horizontal or vertical) arrangement, and each shape was part of only one true pair (Figure 1A, Inventory, True pairs, coloured only for illustrating pair identity).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each shape was part of only one true pair.
source: Unbeknownst to participants, the shapes were grouped into 'true pairs' (the 'objects'), such that constituent shapes of a pair were always shown together and in the same spatial (horizontal or vertical) arrangement, and each shape was part of only one true pair (Figure 1A, Inventory, True pairs, coloured only for illustrating pair identity).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inventory included three horizontal and three vertical true pairs in the visual statistical exposure experiment.
source: The inventory of shapes that could be used for constructing visual scenes included three horizontal and three vertical (visual statistical exposure experiment) or two horizontal and two vertical such true pairs (haptic statistical exposure experiment) as well as an equivalent number of 'pseudo pairs'.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The inventory included two horizontal and two vertical true pairs in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: The inventory of shapes that could be used for constructing visual scenes included three horizontal and three vertical (visual statistical exposure experiment) or two horizontal and two vertical such true pairs (haptic statistical exposure experiment) as well as an equivalent number of 'pseudo pairs'.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each horizontal pseudo pair consisted of two shapes belonging to two different vertical true pairs.
source: The pseudo pairs re-used the shapes of the true pairs such that each horizontal (vertical) pseudo pair consisted of two shapes belonging to two different vertical (horizontal) true pairs, one of them being the top (left) the other the bottom (right) shape of its original true pair (to avoid accidental constellations that could have appeared using true pairs), and each shape was part of only one pseudo pair (Figure 1A, Inventory).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each vertical pseudo pair consisted of two shapes belonging to two different horizontal true pairs.
source: The pseudo pairs re-used the shapes of the true pairs such that each horizontal (vertical) pseudo pair consisted of two shapes belonging to two different vertical (horizontal) true pairs, one of them being the top (left) the other the bottom (right) shape of its original true pair (to avoid accidental constellations that could have appeared using true pairs), and each shape was part of only one pseudo pair (Figure 1A, Inventory).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During visual exposure, only true pairs and no pseudo pairs were shown.
source: During visual exposure, only true pairs and no pseudo pairs were shown.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: During haptic exposure, pseudo pairs were displayed with the same visual statistics as true pairs but they differed in their haptic properties.
source: During haptic exposure, pseudo pairs were displayed with the same visual statistics as true pairs (but they differed in their haptic properties, see below).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The instructions to the participants did not refer to the existence of objects in any way.
source: Crucially, the instructions to the participants did not refer to the existence of objects in any way, only that there were visual or haptic patterns they needed to observe (see also below).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The stimuli were controlled for low-level visual segmentation cues, such that there were no boundaries or colour differences revealing the objects present in a scene.
source: We controlled the stimuli for low-level visual segmentation cues, such that there were no boundaries or colour differences revealing the objects present in a scene (the colour coded shapes in Figure 1A illustrate the construction of scenes but these were never displayed to participants).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The separation between adjacent shapes belonging to the same or different objects was the same and thus uninformative as to object boundaries.
source: Moreover, while individual shapes were clearly separated, the separation between adjacent shapes belonging to the same or different objects was the same and thus uninformative as to object boundaries.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The only information available to identify the objects was the statistics of either their visual co-occurrences or of the physical interactions they afforded across the exposure scenes.
source: Therefore, objects were not defined, as might naively be expected from observing individual scenes, at the level of a single shape or all shapes in a scene. Instead, the only information available to identify the objects was the statistics of either their visual co-occurrences or of the physical interactions they afforded across the exposure scenes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants were exposed to a series of 444 unique scenes in the visual statistical exposure phase.
source: These spatial constraints generated a set of 444 unique scenes, in which each of the 6 pairs appeared 222 times (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each of the 6 pairs appeared 222 times in the visual statistical exposure phase.
source: These spatial constraints generated a set of 444 unique scenes, in which each of the 6 pairs appeared 222 times (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The threshold pulling force was determined for each scene by simulating forces between individual pieces such that pieces belonging to the same object were attached by 11.25 N, and pieces belonging to different objects were attached by 3.75 N.
source: Specifically, the threshold pulling force was determined for each scene by simulating forces between individual pieces such that pieces belonging to the same object were attached by 11.25 N, and pieces belonging to different objects were attached by 3.75 N.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Pulling two objects apart without breaking them required a low force (7.5 N).
source: This meant that pulling two objects apart without breaking them required a low force (7.5 N) whereas breaking each object into two required a high force (22.5 N) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Breaking each object into two required a high force (22.5 N).
source: This meant that pulling two objects apart without breaking them required a low force (7.5 N) whereas breaking each object into two required a high force (22.5 N) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Participants were presented with 48 scenes in total in the haptic pulling test of the visual statistical exposure experiment.
source: Participants were presented with 48 scenes in total (2 × 24-trial blocks).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants performed 72 trials in total in the visual familiarity test of the visual statistical exposure experiment.
source: Participants performed 72 trials (2 × 36-trial blocks) in total.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Pseudo pairs behaved haptically as two separate single-shape objects in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: Critically, pseudo pairs were indistinguishable from true pairs based on their visual appearance statistics: they appeared the same number of times, in the same combinations with the other pairs. This was important so that any consistent preference in the visual familiarity test (see below) between true and pseudo pairs could have only been due to their different haptic statistical properties. Specifically, pseudo pairs behaved haptically as two separate single-shape objects, rather than one integrated object, so that the constituent shapes of a pseudo pair were as easy to pull apart as shapes belonging to two different objects.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Three force levels were required in the haptic statistical exposure experiment: 7.5 N, 15 N, and 22.5 N.
source: This meant that three force levels were required: two true pairs were hard (22.5 N) to pull apart in the direction parallel to their boundary and easy (7.5 N) in the other direction, two pseudo pairs were easy (7.5 N) to pull apart in either direction, and a true and a pseudo pair was easy (7.5 N) to pull apart in the direction orthogonal to the long side of the two pair and medium hard (15 N) in the other direction.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants completed 192 Standard trials in the haptic statistical exposure phase.
source: Participants completed 192 Standard trials (composed of four 48 trial blocks).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants completed 32 trials in the visual familiarity test of the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: Participants completed 32 trials (2 × 16-trial blocks), such that within every 16-trial block each true pair was compared to each pseudo pair of the same orientation in each order exactly once (the order of trials was randomly permuted within each block).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Quantitative debriefing was performed for the final 23 participants at the end of the experiment.
source: Therefore, we chose to perform quantitative debriefing for the final 23 participants at the end of the experiment (16 in the visual and seven in the haptic statistical exposure experiment).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The average pulling force difference between the two levels was 9.3 N ± 3.3 N (s.e.m.) in the visual statistical exposure experiment.
source: The average pulling force difference between the two levels was 9.3 N ± 3.3 N (s.e.m.).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The average pulling force difference between the low and medium breakage force levels was 5.4 N ± 1.2 N (s.e.m.) in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: The average pulling force difference between the low and medium breakage force levels was 5.4 N ± 1.2 N (s.e.m.), and between the medium and high breakage force levels was 2.8 N ± 1.7 N (s.e.m.).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average pulling force difference between the medium and high breakage force levels was 2.8 N ± 1.7 N (s.e.m.) in the haptic statistical exposure experiment.
source: The average pulling force difference between the low and medium breakage force levels was 5.4 N ± 1.2 N (s.e.m.), and between the medium and high breakage force levels was 2.8 N ± 1.7 N (s.e.m.).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.
